why_practices_need.heading: Why Practices Need It
why_practices_need.body_1: Most dental practices manage complex cases without a dedicated system. Case information lives in scattered places: a coordinator's memory, sticky notes, a spreadsheet, and notes buried in the PMS. Problems only surface once they're already expensive.

items.title: Cases tracked in memory:
items.body: The dentist or coordinator knows where things stand, but that knowledge isn't shared. When someone is out sick or busy, cases stall because no one else knows the status.

items.title: No ownership or accountability:
items.body: Multiple people touch a case (hygienist, assistant, coordinator, dentist). But no one is clearly responsible for the next step. Handoffs become drop-offs.

items.title: Delays only noticed after impact:
items.body: By the time someone realizes a case is stalled, the patient has already waited too long, the lab work may need to be redone, or chair time has been wasted.

cases_get_lost.heading: Where Cases Commonly Get Lost or Delayed

steps.title: Between the front desk and the lab
steps.body: A case ships out and the front desk has no visibility into when it's due back or whether it's overdue.

steps.title: Between a referral and the practice
steps.body: A case is sent to a specialist and the loop never formally closes. No one confirms the patient was seen or the next step was completed.

steps.title: Across staff handoffs
steps.body: A case changes hands between team members without a clear record of who owns it next.

steps.title: After a patient reschedule

sections.body_1: A complex dental case is not a single event. A crown, an implant restoration, a bridge, a full-arch case—each one is a small project that runs for weeks, moves between the practice and an outside lab, involves several people, and depends on appointments that may or may not happen when planned.
sections.body_2: Most practices already store plenty of information about those cases. The patient chart is there. The scans are there. The lab slip exists somewhere. What is often missing is something different: an immediate, shared understanding of
sections.body_3: That gap is what visual workflow management addresses. This article explains what a visual dental case workflow is, why it fits multi-stage cases particularly well, what it does not replace, and what to look for if you are evaluating how your practice tracks cases.

complex_dental_cases_are_processes_not_r.heading: Complex Dental Cases Are Processes, Not Records
complex_dental_cases_are_processes_not_r.body_4: This is the distinction that matters most, and it is easy to miss because dental software is generally organized around records.
complex_dental_cases_are_processes_not_r.body_5: A patient record answers questions about a person: what treatment was planned, what was done, what was charged. A case list answers a narrower question: which cases exist. Neither is designed to answer the operational question the team asks all day long—
complex_dental_cases_are_processes_not_r.body_6: what is the state of this work, and what happens next?
complex_dental_cases_are_processes_not_r.body_7: A process has position. At any given moment, a case is somewhere: waiting to be sent, sitting at the lab, back on the shelf waiting to be scheduled, ready to seat. If the system you rely on does not represent that position, then the position lives in someone's memory, in a note, or in a conversation. That is where cases go quiet.

what_a_complex_case_actually_involves.heading: What a Complex Case Actually Involves
what_a_complex_case_actually_involves.body_7: It is worth writing out how much movement a routine lab-based case contains, because the number of transitions is usually higher than it feels:

1.body: The case is initiated after treatment planning or the prep appointment.

2.body: Records are captured—impressions or scans, photos, shade information, prescriptions.

3.body: Information goes out to an external lab, along with instructions and expectations.

4.body: The lab designs the restoration, sometimes returning questions before proceeding.

6.body: The finished work comes back to the practice and has to be received, checked, and stored.

7.body: The patient is scheduled—or rescheduled—for delivery.

8.body: The case is seated, adjusted, and completed.

what_a_complex_case_actually_involves.body_8: It is worth writing out how much movement a routine lab-based case contains, because the number of transitions is usually higher than it feels:
what_a_complex_case_actually_involves.body_9: Between most of those steps there is a handoff: clinical to administrative, practice to lab, lab to practice, administrative to clinical. Each handoff is a point where a case can pause without anyone deciding that it should.

chair_time_has_a_cost.heading: Chair Time Has a Cost
chair_time_has_a_cost.body_3: A dentist's chair time has value whether or not the practice bills specifically for it. When a remake requires a second appointment, the practice gives up an opportunity to see a different patient in that same slot. The value of that time depends on the practice, the type of work typically scheduled in that chair, and the local fee structure.
chair_time_has_a_cost.body_4: For example, a 45-minute remake appointment for a crown has a clear time cost. If a dentist's productive chair time is valued at $500 per hour, the chair time alone for that appointment is over $375. That is in addition to any lab fee or shipping charge.

staff_time_adds_up_too.heading: Staff Time Adds Up Too
staff_time_adds_up_too.body_5: Staff time may be less visible than dentist time, but it is still a real cost. Someone has to coordinate the remake with the patient, communicate with the lab, manage files and records, and update the schedule. For a busy practice, these small tasks accumulate quickly.
staff_time_adds_up_too.body_6: If a staff member spends 20 minutes on a remake at $35 per hour, that is roughly $12 in direct labor per remake. Across dozens of remakes a year, the total becomes meaningful. And that time is also time not spent on other productive or patient-facing work.

dental_case_tracking_checklist.intro: Multi-step dental cases can lose visibility when the information needed to manage them is spread across the PMS, spreadsheets, inboxes, conversations, and staff memory. how_to_use.heading: How to use this checklist
how_to_use.body: Use one checklist record for each active multi-step case. Update the information whenever responsibility, status, next action, or an external dependency changes. Review active cases at a consistent cadence that fits your practice, paying particular attention to handoffs and upcoming patient appointments. Close the case when the operational workflow is actually complete.

about.title: About DentaTrak
about.hero_lead: Dental case tracking built from inside a dental practice.
about.hero_intro: DentaTrak was developed by Dr. William Verrillo, a practicing dentist, after seeing firsthand how easily complex cases can lose visibility as they move between the practice, labs, referrals, follow-ups, and final delivery.
about.origin_title: It started with a simple problem: keeping track of the case after it leaves the chair.
about.origin_body_1: Dr. Verrillo encountered the problem while working with actual dental cases. A patient may have a treatment plan and appointments properly documented in the practice-management system, while the physical case itself is moving through preparation, labs, outside referrals, follow-ups, staff handoffs, due dates, appointments, revisions or remakes, and final delivery.
about.origin_body_2: The challenge is knowing where each case stands across that process. Information can end up distributed across PMS notes, spreadsheets, inboxes, conversations, and staff memory.
about.origin_body_3: The problem often isn't that the information doesn't exist. It's that there isn't one simple operational view showing where the case is, who is responsible, what happens next, whether something is becoming late, and whether the case will be ready for the patient's appointment. DentaTrak was created to solve that.
about.philosophy_title: DentaTrak does one job on purpose.
about.philosophy_body_1: DentaTrak was never intended to replace the practice-management system. A PMS remains responsible for patient records, scheduling, billing, and clinical information.
about.philosophy_body_2: DentaTrak focuses on the operational journey of the case itself: where cases stand, who is responsible, what's coming due, and what needs attention. This focused scope is intentional. DentaTrak complements the systems a practice already uses rather than requiring them to be replaced.
about.closing_title: Built for the way dental cases actually move.

hipaa.baa_heading: A Business Associate Agreement is part of onboarding
hipaa.baa_body: DentaTrak provides a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) as part of practice onboarding. An authorized practice representative must review and accept it before viewing or entering case data. The BAA establishes DentaTrak's responsibilities related to handling protected health information, and the acceptance is recorded in the practice record.
hipaa.baa_existing_customers: If you are an existing practice, you can view your signed BAA from your practice settings. Prospective customers can contact us for more information.
hipaa.safeguards_heading: How DentaTrak protects your practice's information
hipaa.safeguards_lead: DentaTrak combines access controls, encryption, audit logging, and secure session handling to help keep patient information protected.
hipaa.data_protection_body: Sensitive patient information is encrypted before it is stored. Patient names, dates of birth, dentist names, and case notes are encrypted at the application level using AES-256-CBC, and passwords are hashed with bcrypt. All traffic between your browser and DentaTrak is sent over HTTPS.
hipaa.access_controls_body: Users only see information they are authorized to access. Every user is tied to a practice through a membership record, and every request that accesses case data checks that the user belongs to the right practice. Role-based permissions (admin, user, and owner) control what each person can do, and the Assigned Only setting limits a user to seeing only cases assigned to them.
hipaa.files_body: Case attachments are stored in DentaTrak's cloud storage and are never served as public files. Access uses short-lived signed URLs that expire in minutes, and each download request is validated against the user's practice membership and case assignment before the file is streamed.
hipaa.audit_body: DentaTrak records access to protected health information, including who accessed what case, from what IP address, and when. Case status and activity changes are also tracked for accountability and traceability.
hipaa.sessions_body: Sessions are configured with httpOnly, Secure in production, and SameSite=Lax cookies. Sessions time out after 30 minutes of inactivity and are periodically regenerated. Cross-site request forgery tokens are required for state-changing requests, and optional TOTP two-factor authentication is available.
hipaa.retention_heading: Your data isn't trapped in DentaTrak
hipaa.retention_body: Practice data is retained for 7 years after deactivation, which exceeds HIPAA's minimum 6-year requirement. Practice administrators can export practice data at any time through the application.
hipaa.headers_body: DentaTrak uses additional application-level protections and security headers to reduce common web-based risks.
hipaa.shared_responsibility_body: DentaTrak provides technical safeguards and access controls, but each practice also plays an essential role. Your practice remains responsible for how staff use the system, who receives access, account security, devices and networks, training, and its own HIPAA policies and procedures. Using DentaTrak does not, by itself, make a practice HIPAA compliant.
hipaa.practice_responsibilities_heading: What your practice is responsible for
hipaa.practice_responsibilities_body: DentaTrak provides the technical controls, but your practice is responsible for managing users, protecting credentials, and following your own policies and procedures.
hipaa.responsibilities_item_1: Remove access when staff leave or change roles.
hipaa.responsibilities_item_4: Access DentaTrak from appropriately secured devices and networks.
hipaa.responsibilities_item_5: Train staff on your practice's privacy and HIPAA procedures.
